description_full: Grupo Simec, S.A.B. de C.V. produces, processes, and distributes special steels and structural steel profiles in Mexico, the United States, Canada, and Brazil. It offers steel wire and derivatives, special bar quality steel, rebar, and commercial and structural long products. The company was founded in 1969 and is headquartered in Guadalajara, Mexico. Grupo Simec, S.A.B. de C.V. is a subsidiary of Industrias CH, S.A.B. de C.V.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 4K people. Revenue per employee of $373K ranks in the bottom quartile among Basic Materials peers. Each employee generates $38K of free cash flow annually.
financial_summary: Grupo Simec, S.A.B. de C.V. is a mid-cap basic materials business with a $4.0B market cap on $1.8B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at -12% over the past three years, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome. Operating margins are expanding by +4.2pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.

Returns on capital run at 29% against a 8% cost of capital — a 21-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 23% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $188M in free cash flow — roughly 10 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.53×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 0.2%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.

sect: Its 37% operating margin runs 28pp above the Basic Materials median (10%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.84x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.1% of sector revenue and 0.3% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+39.6% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.04 across 219 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 25% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 44% and a beta of 0.50, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.87 vs 5y 0.29), so read it loosely.
Trading is thin (about $42K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 45% in the 2020 crash, 22% in the 2022 bear market and 81% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 37% below its DCF fair value of $41.50, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 28%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $35.17 to $50.35 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Basic Materials peers: P/E 22.0 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 33% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.7% (below the risk-free rate).
The price implies 6.0% annual cash-flow growth, 11pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 29% clears the cost of capital of 8.0% by 21pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.65).
It runs a 23% gross margin and converts 10% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: cash conversion of only 0.53x.
ROE of 20% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.2x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 19pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $1.4B.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 6.3, in the safe zone).
The Beneish M-score (-2.18) sits just under the manipulation line, so earnings quality bears watching.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -12.3% over 3 years and 0.8% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 28%).
At current returns, reinvesting 22% of profits supports about 6.4% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.0%), and institutions hold 0%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.2% (0.2% in buybacks).
people: With about 4,961 employees, each generates about $373K of revenue, 0.6x the Basic Materials median.
That works out to $38K of free cash flow per employee.
